To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the temperature dependence of NO laser-induced fluorescence in the range 1500-2150K can be described by a model in which the quenching corrections can be neglected, and that the absolute NO concentration can be measured with a relative error of 5% using the calibration procedure presented.

the temperature dependence of the laser-induced NO A?(+)-X? fluorescence is described by the temperature-dependent Boltzmann distribution, that the quenching corrections can be neglected for millijoule excitation energies, and that the calibration of NO concentration in flames is possible by the use of the seeded flame method.
the temperature dependence of NO A (2) fluorescence is best described by a two-level model, and that the NO concentration can be measured with a relative accuracy of about 5% using this method.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of laser-based techniques for the measurement of the absolute concentration and temperature profiles in premixed flames.
a study of the temperature dependence of laser-excited fluorescence of nitric oxides in laminar premixtured atmospheric pressure flames.
the determination of absolute NO concentrations in the hot gases above a flat-flame burner by means of laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the present excitation conditions, the NO A(2)?(+) -X(2)? fluorescence intensity is a linear function of the NO concentration, and that the temperature dependence is well described by the model of a saturated two-state system.
, under the experimental conditions used, the quenching of NO fluorescence is negligible.

, in premixed, atmospheric-pressure flames, the temperature dependence of the NO fluorescence intensity is well described by a simple model, which neglects quenching, if millijoule pulses are used and the NO is not in a highly excited vibrational state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the temperature dependence of NO fluorescence in premixed atmospheric-pressure hydrocarbon flames can be described satisfactorily by the temperature-dependent quenching model, if the NO seed concentration is known.
the temperature dependence of NO laser-induced fluorescence in the A-X system can be used to measure NO concentrations in atmospheric pressure flames.
the calibration factor for the NO A (2)?(+)-X ( 2 )? fluorescence is a constant, which depends on the excitation energy, but is independent of the local gas composition and temperature.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the calibration of laser-induced fluorescence measurements of NO concentration in flames can be achieved by seeding the flame with a known quantity of NO, provided that the seed is not allowed to burn.

, in order to determine the temperature from the NO A (2) fluorescence intensity at a fixed excitation pulse energy, the quenching corrections have to be taken into account, which is not the case when the pulse energy is increased.

the NO concentration in the hot gases can be determined with millijoule laser pulse energies, without the need to know the local temperature, by using the temperature dependence of the fluorescence intensity.
